item.title: The Joy of Writing
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Joy of Writing

We shouldn't let AI do our work for us, for many reasons.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Writing is challenging, and while making that effort is hard, it's also valuable.
  • AI has its appropriate uses, but we should focus on creating our own work first.
  • One good use of AI may be as a sparring partner to help vet ideas.
Writing can be effortful, but of high value, too.
Source: Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication.

I began writing a paper the other day; laid out my plan for the "story" and set about pulling the introduction together. I hit roadblocks here and there, struggled to find the right expression for the ideas floating around in my head, paused, stood up and paced, started up again, and eventually packed it up to be dealt with in my next writing session.

And at some point, it occurred to me: I like this. I find this fun. There is joy in the challenging process of writing.

Now I am not anti-AI. I have used it for a variety of purposes. (I will say I am against the theft of work to build AI models, whether that be written work or visual art, and I will be a beneficiary of the successful lawsuit against Anthropic after they stole my book co-authored with John Eastwood, Out of My Skull.)

But I do think we lose something if we give up tasks to large language models (LLMs) that we could do ourselves.

Downsides of Using AI

First, we become more boring. I have written about this elsewhere. LLMs are data-hungry, predictive algorithms. It's that predictive nature that makes them implant the most probable word in any given sentence. As Mark Bieleke and Wanja Wolff recently highlighted, this will essentially be regression to the mean; we will all begin to sound alike. Imagine if literature did this? All novels reading like they were written by Dan Brown? (You could choose an author you liked more; and to be clear, I have never read a Dan Brown book, but the idea is the same—reading would become pretty boring if all you had available were Stephen King books—and I love King’s work).

Second, when we divest the task of writing to AI, we forego the joy of striving. Cognitive scientists have generally suggested that, all things being equal, we tend to want to avoid effort—even effortful thinking. That is, we are cognitive misers. This makes a lot of biological sense—the resources we need to function (e.g., glucose, oxygen) are not unlimited, and so we ought to conserve them, and avoiding more effortful tasks is one way to do that.

But Michael Inzlicht has recently suggested a different account of effort—that it can feel good to do something effortful. This might be because at the end of the process, we have a sense of achievement. In essence, there can be no pleasure without some pain. I think of tattoos. We like the etchings we choose to leave on our skin not merely for their aesthetics and personal relevance, but also because we survived the self-inflicted torture of getting them in the first place.

But Inzlicht goes a step further—sometimes we choose things because they are effortful. We know beforehand this thing we’re choosing to do will be hard. But we do it anyway, because we place value on effort. Perhaps it says something about us that we can soldier through.

Third, if we let AI be our only writing tool, we abdicate the responsibility for developing our own skills and our own voice. This is similar to the complaint that we all start to sound alike and become mind-numbingly boring to read. It’s the flipside of that claim.

article continues after advertisement

Most of us exposed to Psych 101 classes are aware of the magical 7 ±2 number, or Miller's Law. This is supposedly the amount of information we can keep in mind over a short period of time (our short-term, or working memory capacity). But you should read the introductory paragraph of the original paper by George A. Miller. He describes being paranoid, being constantly “persecuted” by a number, evoking possible conspiracy theories to explain why "seven" seems to be dogging him, peeking out from every corner of data he ever looks at. It’s brilliant: quirky, funny, engaging, and essentially Miller’s voice. (As an aside, I think we have become less tolerant of this kind of tongue-in-cheek approach in scientific writing, and we are worse off for it).

If we let AI and LLMs do our writing for us, there is little chance we will find our own, unique voice. Indeed, recent work suggests that using AI to write leads us to adopt the catchphrases and buzzwords that AI tends to prefer in our own speech. We are not just beginning to sound alike; we are sounding like AI, and this should disturb us.

So what are we to do? Given the prevalence of LLMs and the ease with which students and teachers alike can lean on them, it would seem ridiculous to suggest we abandon them. The genie is well and truly out of the bottle (and, according to some hyperbole, is a good chance to kill us within the decade).

Some Better Uses for AI in Writing

My first suggestion would be to stop avoiding the pain. Anything worthwhile takes effort, not just writing. Our relationships, our hobbies, and even such mundanities as our gardens and looking after our pets. All take effort, and all are worthwhile. Expressing your ideas without external help is of enormous value. It forces you to crystallize the ideas in your head, and as the words unfold on the page (sometimes chaotically, sometimes painfully slowly), you are forced to challenge that crystallization. Am I getting that point quite right? Will it be understood the way I want it to be? How will others challenge it?

article continues after advertisement

Second, by all means use AI to help clean up your writing. My grammar (this post is likely a great example) is not exemplary. I have colleagues for whom English is their second language who have a far better grasp of the split infinitive than I do. Especially for scientists for whom English is their second language, LLMs can be particularly helpful. But I do think the process should begin with our own, human ideas, however effortful they are to develop and express.

Essentially, writing is about sharing ideas. Once written and shared, your ideas no longer belong to you—they are there for the world to debate, deconstruct, and absorb into their own thinking. One recent suggested use of AI seems particularly useful to me in this context. In a recent Nature paper, Marc Schmitt suggested using LLMs as sparring partners. Present your ideas and your arguments, and ask Claude to prove you wrong. I do still believe that we get a wide range of things from person-to-person conversation that Chatbots can never replace. But this strikes me as a sensible use of the tool.

Beyond avoiding the pain of writing, I would also say to embrace the joy. I find it exciting to engage in the hard work of putting pen to paper. But maybe that’s just me.

item.title: Are FaceTime Calls to the Other Parent Always a Good Idea?
item.description:
Parenting

Are FaceTime Calls to the Other Parent Always a Good Idea?

Consider your child's experience when planning co-parenting communication.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Phone calls are put in place to support the child’s connection with both parents.
  • Parental tension can turn a well-intended phone call into a stressful experience for their child.
  • If required calls consistently cause distress, be open to an adjustment.

Q: My son goes back and forth between his mother and me every few days. He’s 4. Although his mother and I don’t agree about much, we miss him when he’s not with us, so we asked for a FaceTime call every night to be added to his custody order. Lately, I’ve noticed that he gets anxious when it’s time to call his mother, and tonight, he said he didn’t want to talk to her. I don’t know what’s going on. What should we do?

A: It’s quite common for parenting plans to incorporate a phone or FaceTime call when the child is with the other parent. The idea is that a call will help the child feel close to both parents as they go back and forth between homes.

I’m going to go out on a limb here and say it’s not my favorite approach. Of course, there are times when it works well, particularly with long-distance co-parenting, when the parent and child don’t see each other for weeks or even months at a time. But if the child goes back and forth between parents every few days, strictly scheduled phone calls may interrupt their ability to calmly settle into a routine at their other home.

When I see phone calls become the most disruptive is when the parents are barely talking to each other, and they are required to coordinate a call so the child can touch base with the other parent. This can be especially troublesome when the child is too young to manage the call without help—about your son’s age or younger. These parents must hold the phone and prompt the child to speak, even when they would rather not interact with each other. Some struggle to keep their animosity out of the exchange and have told me they feel the calls are just another way for the other parent to spy on them. When that’s the thinking going into a call, it’s difficult to create a relaxed, positive experience for the child. Simply anticipating the interaction can bring on anxiety for both parents and especially their child.

Based on that, is it really surprising that after a time, the child balks at making phone calls? It can be the same reason some children say they don’t want to go to the other parent’s home. It’s not necessarily what the other parent is doing that prompts the child to say, "No." Sometimes, it’s the tension between the parents, and the child is really saying, “Enough!”

So, do some soul-searching before you demand that a phone or FaceTime call be part of your child's parenting plan. Is the phone call for you or for the child? If the child must check in every day with the other parent, it may not allow them to settle in. Each call can make them revisit their parents’ breakup—every day, with every phone call. The calls can work against the child when the requirement takes priority over how the child is experiencing them.

Now, when parents approach calls cooperatively, a phone call here and there can be a fun way to check in. Send the other parent a pic of gymnastics practice, and the child might initiate a return phone call afterward for some positive reinforcement. Or, if the child requests to speak to the other parent, that’s a cue to help make the connection. When you hear your child's voice, a soothing response might be, “Hey, buddy! It’s great to hear your voice!” Not, “Oh my gosh, I miss you so much. Life just isn’t the same when you’re not here.” Although you might truly feel that way, sharing those feelings can add to his anxiety. He may feel caught between the two people he loves the most: “Mom (or Dad) misses me, and I can’t be there.” Think of the pressure this puts on a child.

article continues after advertisement

Tips to Make FaceTime Calls Go More Smoothly

The success of intermittent phone calls depends largely on how parents manage them. If you are determined to incorporate calls into the parenting plan, consider these tips to help them go more smoothly:

  • Don’t play games or look for ways to prevent your child from connecting with their other parent.
  • Honor scheduled call times, while allowing reasonable flexibility when your child’s activities or needs require it.
  • Find a comfortable place for calls, but there’s no need to exile your child to a back room. Normalize the interaction. Aim for a positive atmosphere with enough privacy for your child to feel at ease.
  • Don’t turn calls into a bone of contention. Remember, your child did not choose to live in two homes, and coordinating calls is not their responsibility.
  • If your child asks to speak to the other parent during your parenting time, help make that happen.
  • Check your attitude when it’s time for a call. Your child can pick up on your negativity, which can make transitions harder and interfere with their ability to settle in.
  • Keep calls appropriate to your child’s age and attention span. A 4-year-old may want to show you a toy, say goodnight, and get back to playing. A short call can still be a good call.
  • Take an interest without conducting an interview. “What was fun today?” invites conversation. Questions about the other parent’s activities or visitors put your child in the middle.
  • Keep adult business between adults. A call with your child is not the time to discuss schedules, money, or disagreements with the other parent.
  • Give your child permission to enjoy the other home. “Have fun with Mom!” or “Enjoy your evening with Dad!” lets your child know that being happy there is okay.
  • End warmly, without guilt. “I loved talking with you. See you Saturday!” offers reassurance without making your child responsible for how much you miss them.
  • If calls consistently upset your child, take that seriously. Discuss the pattern with the other parent at a separate time, away from your child, and focus on what would make the contact more comfortable.

If a call is required, it’s up to the parents to make it a positive experience for their child. If they consistently struggle to do that, it’s time to seek a change to the arrangement rather than keep putting the child through a stressful exchange. The purpose of the call is to support the child’s relationship with both parents, and that purpose should guide how the adults handle it.

Phone calls can be a great way to touch base if the parents handle the interaction collaboratively. If they reach out to one another, reinforcing each other’s place in their child’s life, then a phone or FaceTime call is a great way to ensure continuity and predictability. But if a phone call is put in place to establish territory or out of insecurity—“I’m afraid he might forget about me”—it can leave the child trying to soothe a parent’s anxiety rather than receiving help managing his own.

item.title: From Working With AI to Connecting With People
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

From Working With AI to Connecting With People

Building a transition ritual matters for better communication.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • AI communication lacks courtesy; humans need emotional intelligence and patience.
  • Inefficiencies in human interaction build relationships and improve future teamwork.
  • Engaging one's senses to transition from AI mode to human conversations creates effective interactions.
Source: Yankruk/Pexels

You’ve been locked in with AI for the last hour. “No, shorter.” “Try again.” “That’s not what I meant.” “Go back to the first version.” No greeting or thank-yous change the conversation. It’s not necessary to soften your feedback or wonder if you hurt its feelings. You’ve covered an impressive amount of ground, and everything has moved at your pace.

Then, you close the window and walk into a meeting with actual people. Someone wants to tell you about their weekend. Another person needs more context. Someone starts brainstorming when you thought you were there to make a decision. You can feel yourself getting impatient. The gears have shifted, and suddenly, you can’t get what you want at the pace that you want it anymore. There are complexities, nonverbal communication to decode, and emotions alongside the words. Now you’re dealing with humans, and humans require something different from you.

We already know this, of course. We naturally adjust how we communicate depending on who is in front of us. You probably don’t talk to your boss exactly the way you talk to your best friend, and you may not talk to the person who cuts your hair the way you talk to your partner. Different relationships bring out different parts of us and require different levels of patience, context, humor, restraint, and awareness. This is part of the art of human conversation. We read tone and nonverbals. We remember what went well last time and what didn’t, and that helps us adjust.

With AI entering our interactions in all kinds of ways these days, we have another communication mode to adapt to. But this one is fundamentally different for one obvious reason: AI isn’t human. Most of you reading this have probably had some kind of back-and-forth with AI, whether it was helping you plan a long weekend getaway, organize your thoughts, draft something, or build agents that take tasks off your team’s plate. Many of us have welcomed AI into our work and lives to carry out a task, a function, or many.

When we are working with AI, there is very little common courtesy required because AI doesn’t demand it. We don’t experience the same negative consequences if we immediately show frustration, skip the pleasantries, interrupt, change direction abruptly, or disappear from the conversation altogether. In that mode of communication, everything adapts to us. AI is constantly adjusting to us, which is very different from human-to-human interaction.

Moving From AI to Human Meetings

Having a meeting with one coworker versus another requires you to access your emotional intelligence. You’re decoding how they entered the space and noticing their tone. You’ve learned that with this person, checking in first goes a long way. With someone else, getting right to the point works better. These seemingly small interactions build cohesion and trust and can sometimes soothe the hesitation or anxiety someone brought into the room with them.

article continues after advertisement
Source: Yankruk/Pexels

With AI, you can jump right in and jump right out. You are also largely in the lead. You decide where the conversation goes, when it changes direction, how much context you provide, when you interrupt, and when you’re finished. If the response isn’t quite on your wavelength, you redirect it, and AI adjusts. When you move back into a conversation with another person, you are no longer the only one setting the pace. You have to share the spotlight. You may have an agenda, but so do they. They may need more context when you feel like you are already 10 steps ahead.

If you have just spent an hour intensely working with AI, that difference can be jarring. You may notice yourself becoming impatient. Your listening skills may not be fully firing. You might interrupt more quickly or feel irritated by a conversation that seems to be taking too long to get somewhere. That doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve suddenly become an impatient person or that your coworker is inefficient. You may just not have transitioned yet.

There is another piece here, too. An intense working session with AI can be incredibly productive, but productive doesn’t necessarily mean mentally restful. You may have covered an enormous amount of ground in a short period of time, making decisions, evaluating information, redirecting, refining, generating ideas, and staying deeply focused. The task may have become more efficient while your brain has still been working hard. Then you close the window and immediately ask yourself to listen, collaborate, read another person, regulate your own reactions, and tolerate a much less predictable pace. You may simply be drained.

Building a Transitional Ritual

We already understand the importance of transitions in other parts of our lives. Athletes warm up before competing. Many of us have rituals that help us move from work mode into home mode. We give ourselves time to settle into new environments. But we don’t necessarily think about transitioning between two completely different forms of interaction while sitting at the same desk. You can close an AI working session at 1:59 and enter a Zoom meeting at 2:00, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the rest of you made the transition that quickly.

article continues after advertisement

So, build one in. It doesn’t have to be elaborate. Stand up, look away from the screen, get some water, and move your body. Give yourself a minute without another input or output and recognize what you are transitioning into. Engage your senses and check in with yourself: Who am I about to talk with? Am I prepared to listen and change my pace? Can I tolerate this conversation unfolding differently than I would structure it? Am I ready to share the lead?

Valuing Human Interaction's Inefficiencies

That last question may be particularly important because human interaction is inefficient sometimes. We repeat ourselves, tell stories, shoot the sh*t. We misread each other, and sometimes our conversations go nowhere. We need clarification; we pause, circle back, and sometimes need a little banter before getting to the point. But some of that “inefficiency” is also where relationships are built. It’s where we learn how someone thinks, what makes them laugh, what makes them hesitate, and what they need from us. Those pieces of information become the data that help us work better together the next time.

The goal isn’t to make our interactions with AI more human or to stop using the efficiency it offers. It is to recognize that when we leave that environment, the rules change. AI can meet you where you are almost instantly. Human interaction asks more of both people. We have to listen, adjust, tolerate some friction, share the lead, and meet each other somewhere in the middle. Being intentional about that transition may help us get the benefits of working with AI without bringing the expectations of that interaction into the relationships that still require us to be imperfectly human.

item.title: What Is Your Child Learning From You About Technology Use?
item.description:
Parenting

What Is Your Child Learning From You About Technology Use?

It’s not just kids' screen time that matters—parents’ usage matters, too.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • When it comes to screen time, parents may be modeling the same behaviors they’re trying to limit.
  • Parents tend to be less responsive and sensitive to children's bids for attention when on devices.
  • Research finds parental technology use in children's presence is associated with a range of negative outcomes.
Source: Ron Lach / Pexels

Today’s parents are continually looking for the best ways to manage their children’s technology use. Much of the conversation has focused on children's screen time: How much screen time is too much? What content are they watching? What limits should be put in place?

More recent recommendations, including those from the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), have moved away from strict time-based guidelines towards recommendations for creating healthy media habits. Nevertheless, most recommendations still offer little guidance for parental screen use, despite emerging research suggesting this could be a part of the equation. An important question to explore then is: What are children learning about technology from watching their parents use it?

Impact of Parental Phone Use on Child Interactions

Young children constantly make bids for connection by asking their parents questions, telling stories, needing help, and seeking reassurance. The way a parent responds to these bids is foundational in building a strong parent-child relationship. Unfortunately, research shows it can interfere with responsive interaction.

In a recent observational study of parents interacting with their young children, researchers found that when parents were using their phones, they were about five times less likely to respond to their children's bids for attention. And when they did respond, their responses were less timely and engaged.

Effects of Parental Phubbing on Children

Source: Gustavo Fring / Pexels

This helps explain why researchers have become interested in the concept of parental phubbing, which refers to the act of parents using mobile phones in the presence of their children instead of engaging with them. A 2023 review of 42 studies involving 56,275 children found that parental phubbing was associated with children’s internalizing problems (e.g., depression and anxiety) and externalizing problems (e.g., aggression and conduct problems), as well as lower self-esteem and social-emotional competence (e.g., ability to understand and express emotions and relationship skills).

These results were expanded in a 2026 study of 600 teens who demonstrated higher levels of attachment insecurity to both mother and father figures when parents focused on their phones during attempts to connect.

Source: August de Richelieu / Pexels

Influence of Parental Tech Use on Children's Tech Habits

Research on parental technoference, technology-related interruptions and interference to family interactions, has found connections between parents' device usage and that of their children. A 2025 meta-analysis reviewed 53 studies with more than 60,000 participants. Results suggested a significant association between parental technoference and children’s problematic media use, with stronger associations when both parents engaged in technoference. In other words, parents' technology behavior isn't only potentially impacting the quality of the interaction; it may also impact children's own relationship with technology.

This body of research adds another dimension to the story. Parents are modeling what a relationship with technology looks like to their children. As such, parents may inadvertently model that screen-based interactions are prioritized over physical interaction, boredom can be filled through screens, and other problematic behaviors.

Developmental and Relational Implications of Parental Screen Use

A 2026 study published in JAMA Pediatrics demonstrated that primary parent smartphone screen time was associated with slower growth in children's receptive vocabulary from ages 5 to 7. Each additional hour of daily parental smartphone screen time was associated with slightly slower growth in children’s receptive vocabulary scores.

Furthermore, a 2025 review of 21 studies including nearly 15,000 participants found that parental technology use in children's presence was associated with a range of outcomes, including poorer cognitive development, more internalizing and externalizing behaviors, less prosocial behavior, weaker parent-child attachment, and greater child screen use.

Importantly, most research on impacts of parental technology use is correlational with small effect sizes, so findings cited here do not establish that parental screen use causes developmental or behavioral problems in children. Rather, they suggest that what happens during parental screen use may influence children’s developmental and relational experiences.

Strategies for Families to Manage Technology Use

We can look to countries such as Sweden, which has broader recommendations that include adults and parents. As of June 2026, Sweden’s public health authority released new recommendations for screen exposure and use, including for parents. Parental recommendations include:

Source: August de Richelieu / Pexels
  • Recognize that your own screen behavior can influence children's habits.
  • Put phones away when spending time with children, using devices around children primarily when necessary.
  • Create screen-free zones in the home.

The significance of this approach is not that parents should follow a particular set of rules, nor is it indicating that parents need to be device-free. Instead, it expands the focus beyond how much screen time children should get to ask when, why, and how screens are being used within the whole family. Creating device-free periods of undivided attention, such as during mealtime, bedtime, conversations, play, and moments when a child is actively seeking connection, may be one practical way to be more intentional about technology use and model the relationship with devices we hope to foster in our children. Ultimately, children's technology habits develop within a relational and family context, and parents are an important part to consider.

item.title: Tickling: The Good and the Bad
item.description:
Laughter

Tickling: The Good and the Bad

The science of why we do, and do not, like tickling.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Tickling is usually thought of as play behavior, but not everyone likes it.
  • Laughing and smiling don't always indicate positive emotion.
  • Tickling, and the laughter and squirming that results, may have evolved to help protect us from attack.

Is tickling simply playful behavior or is there more to it? In another example of how we are all different, many people interpret tickling as an act of aggression or interpret the tickle as painful and not play at all. And yet, these same tickle-haters likely behave as tickle aficionados do, smiling and laughing when tickled. So, why do we tend to respond with signals that usually indicate positive emotion, even if we don’t like what elicited them?

Smiles

Humans smile when they are amused, but also in very different, even negative situations. Harris and Alvarado (2005) asked people about their emotional responses to three different conditions. First, being tickled. Second, listening to a recording of a comedy sketch and third, having their left hand immersed in a cold-water bath (a painful condition that the participants endured only for as long as they wanted to). The researchers also recorded the facial expressions of the participants in all three conditions. Finally, the participants were asked about their emotional response to each of the conditions and if they enjoyed being tickled.

Guillaume-Benjamin-Amand Duchenne (de Boulogne) embarked on the first scientific, systematic exploration of the physiology of human facial expression and hoped, through photographs of the experiments, to teach artists how to portray those emotions. This natural smile has come to be known as Duchenne’s Smile
Source: Cleveland Museum of Art, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

About a third of the participants (32%) said they enjoyed being tickled, another 32% had a mixed reaction to it and about 36% said they did not like it at all. When they compared facial expressions across the three conditions, both tickling and listening to comedy elicited a true “Duchenne’s Smile” – an upward turn of the lips and crinkling of the skin around the eyes – the kind of smile that is usually taken as a genuine indication of positive emotion. Non-Duchenne smiles involve only the mouth, and can indicate politeness, dominance, embarrassment, even anxiety. Duchenne’s smiles were correlated with self-report of positive emotion and were most likely to be seen when listening to comedy, less likely when being tickled, and never shown when experiencing pain. Non-Duchenne’s smiles were generally equally frequent across all three conditions.

Laughter

Laughing is ubiquitous and universal in humans, appearing across age and culture. It is perhaps the first social behavior to appear in human infants, with smiling appearing at around two months followed by laughter emerging at roughly three months of age (Kennison, 2020). It has been documented in primates in general, as well as in non-primates, even in rats (Gloveli, Simonnet, Tang, et al., 2023). Laughing is apparently innate and reflexive, appearing without learning and without hearing or seeing another member of our own species demonstrating it for us. Congenitally blind children smile never having seen a smile before (Kinnison, 2020), and congenitally deaf children laugh without ever having heard the peculiar sounds before (Provine and Emmorey, 2006).

article continues after advertisement

The structure of laughter is the same across human beings as well. Provine (1996) says, “A laugh is characterized by a series of short, vowel like notes (syllables), each about 75 milliseconds long, that are repeated at regular intervals, each about 210 milliseconds apart.” (p. 39).

However, some research suggests that laughs evoked by different triggering stimuli can be distinguished by listeners. Kamiloğlu, Sun, et al., (2024) recorded laughter evoked by four different types of triggers: being tickled, watching a comedy sketch, seeing someone else’s misfortune (Schadenfreude) like accidentally pouring salt into coffee instead of sugar, and hearing a verbal joke. They then asked 201 volunteers to listen to clips of laughter and to classify them according to triggering stimulus. Participants were significantly better at identifying laughter evoked by tickling than by non-tickling contexts. The laugh elicited by tickling sounded different than did non-tickle laughs. Another set of participants were asked to listen to the same laughter sets and to rate on a 7-point Likert scale the level of arousal, positive emotion and voice control in each laugh. Laughter produced by tickling was rated as indicating significantly more arousal than other laughs and as significantly less controlled.

It turns out that this last finding may be related to why some people don’t care for tickling.

Theories of tickling

Gregory (1924) suggested that tickling and the responses it most often evokes, laughter and squirming, may have evolved to help protect us from attack. A reflexive response practiced through play when we are children. He points out that the ticklish spots on our bodies (the side of the waist, the armpits and neck, the soles of the feet) are spots that are only rarely “touched in peace, but they are significantly, points of attack in war.” (p. 49) The squirming we do when tickled may be a reflexive escape response, practiced since childhood. The laugh that tickling evokes may also be reflexive and out of our control. Remember that part of the distinctive sound signature of tickle-evoked laughter is the lack of control.

Laughter and smiling are social signals, usually letting other people know that we’re engaged with them, that we are not a threat, and sometimes, that we would like a repeat of whatever evoked them. However, laughter and smiles can also indicate other more negative emotional states like embarrassment or pain. Gregory (1924) points out that tickling a child who suspects you or fears you, will elicit a squirm, but not a laugh. Individual differences in the perception of the intensity of the tickle or differences in the level of trust the ticklee has in the tickler, or differences in personality or mood, may affect how we interpret the touch and the tickle (Kilteni, 2025).

The real art of tickling may actually lie in being able to tell when enough is enough.

item.title: Why Are We So Bad at Resisting a Craving?
item.description:
Diet

Why Are We So Bad at Resisting a Craving?

Two very different factors influence our self-control.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Maintaining willpower in the face of a craving may depend on how "loud" the craving is.
  • GLP-1 medications may quiet the craving itself.
  • Fake delivery apps offer the pleasure of anticipation without eating.

It’s 9:45 p.m. The kids have finally fallen asleep. You had a long day. Your Instagram feed keeps showing you tempting recipes, but your fridge is full of leftovers, and you want something warm and comforting. You can almost smell it. You open the delivery app and scroll. You see the hamburger in front of your eyes; you can smell the fries, and you want the milkshake, too. Even before you complete the purchase, you know exactly how you’ll feel after eating the food, but right now, you don’t care.

This strong urge is what made a 21-year-old engineering student in Seoul build a delivery website that allows you to scroll through menus, fill your cart, place your order, track the courier on the map, and… that’s it. You don’t have to pay, and you don’t get the food. According to a New York Times article, more than 10,000 people visit the website every month. Why would someone do that? Are we enjoying the expectation or the food itself?

When the Wanting Is Better Than the Eating

In reward research, wanting something and enjoying it are two different things. Wanting is the pull toward something; enjoyment is the pleasure we get when we actually have it. Usually, we enjoy the anticipation that comes before getting it: a new book we’ve downloaded, a new dress, or the hamburger that is on its way to us. We look for it, we want it, and then we get it. But sometimes, as soon as it’s there, or right after we eat it, it doesn’t make us happy. Sometimes it makes us sad, disappointed, or empty.

We tend to judge ourselves regarding the second part of the process; not the wanting as much as the consumption itself. But when we get to the moment of consumption, it is usually after the process of expectation has been underway for a while.

What If the Wanting Gets Quieter?

Using that notion, the fake delivery apps are keeping the entire expectation part and removing the last part, trying to satisfy the wanting without the actual eating. Some of these apps give you a total of the money or calories you’ve saved as a reward. But the satisfaction is still very limited.

GLP-1 medications offer the opposite. If the fake delivery apps suggest keeping the wanting part and removing the eating, GLP-1 works, in part, by changing the craving itself.

In a 2015 study, researchers gave 48 participants a GLP-1 medication and measured their brain activity while they anticipated and received chocolate milk. What they discovered was reduced responses associated with anticipating the food, and increased responses when the chocolate milk arrived. The drink intake itself was lower compared to participants who didn’t receive GLP-1.

article continues after advertisement

This is a small study, and it doesn’t tell us that anyone taking GLP-1 will experience it that way, but these results are interesting. The medication changed the pull of the drink before it arrived. The expectation was lower; the constant food noise wasn’t so loud.

This sounds a lot like the way GLP-1 users describe their experience. Instead of the internal struggle, “I wish I could drink this, but I know I shouldn’t have it,” the noise is quieter. The drink is there, I could have it, and I don’t really care.

The effect of craving less is noticeable in what these people buy. A study in the Journal of Marketing Research showed that within 6 months of starting GLP-1, households reduced grocery spending by 5.3 percent. Spending at fast-food restaurants, coffee shops, and other limited-service restaurants fell by 8 percent, and spending on savory snacks fell by 10.1 percent. When households stopped the medication, their spending moved back toward pre-medication levels.

Is Appetite Really a Character Test?

We tend to judge others, and ourselves, as lacking in discipline when we can’t resist the hamburger or the chocolate milk. We feel like we don’t have enough willpower. We assume that everyone experiences wanting in a similar way, but what if they don’t? The intensity of the desire makes a real difference. We ask people to apply self-control, to work harder and stronger, to commit, to “just do it,” but we rarely ask how loud the noise they hear is.

Maybe what we call a willpower problem is actually a problem of a stronger pull? While fake delivery apps give people the anticipation without the reward, GLP-1s quiet down the anticipation.

It’s easier for us to look at the bottom line and judge our self-control and willpower, but it might be interesting and useful to look at how loud the wanting is in the first place.

item.title: Those Symptoms May Be Perimenopause
item.description:
Menopause

Those Symptoms May Be Perimenopause

Perimenopause can begin earlier and show up in more ways than many realize.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Perimenopause symptoms go far beyond hot flashes and irregular periods.
  • Perimenopausal changes can begin earlier than many women expect.
  • Recognizing unexpected perimenopause symptoms can help women start the right conversation with their doctor.

My mother told me about menstruation, and my grandmother told me about menopause, but nobody told me about perimenopause. Research and conversations with my patients tell me that not much has changed. Many women say they are still unclear about the terminology, the symptoms, and the timing of perimenopause, and were surprised when their doctors said their "problems" were related to perimenopause.

The two signs of perimenopause that are well recognized are irregular menstrual cycles and hot flashes, day or night. They are both vasomotor changes caused by hormonal shifts leading toward a final menstrual cycle. Twelve months after that final period, we are officially in menopause. But there are many other perimenopause changes that are less obvious, and because so many assume perimenopause doesn’t begin until a woman is in her late 40s, the symptoms are written off as fatigue or stress. Actually, about 30 percent of women who consult a doctor about perimenopause-related symptoms are aged 30–451, so here are some less-known symptoms that may be associated with perimenopause.

Burning Mouth/Dry Tongue

Hormonal changes during perimenopause affect all the body’s mucous membranes, and that includes the oral epithelium (the inside of the mouth). If it thins or atrophies, it’s more easily scratched and painfully irritated. Saliva glands may also be compromised, and a dry mouth means increased susceptibility to yeast infections, nerve sensitivity, gum disease, and pain without obvious injury, often called burning mouth syndrome. Your dentist will help by recommending rinses, medications, and a diet to keep your mouth comfortable and free of infection.2

Dry Eyes

If you wear contact lenses and need more eye drops and time-out from your lenses than just a few years ago, perimenopause may be contributing. Tear glands, natural eye lubrication, and resistance to inflammation and irritation are all affected by changes in estrogen levels. Hormone receptors also affect cornea, lens, and retina fluid levels. Check with your ophthalmologist before assuming the problem is allergies or computer eye fatigue.3

The "Sneeze Squeeze"

Since the pelvic floor muscles and urethral control can both weaken during perimenopause, quickly crossing your legs and contracting your pelvic floor when you laugh or sneeze can become a reflex to stop urinary leaks and embarrassment. Kegel exercises to strengthen your pelvic floor muscles may help, but if bladder leaks become a significant inconvenience, your physician can recommend treatment and management.4

Heart Palpitations

Did you know that about 40 percent of perimenopausal women experience heart palpitations? Those who don’t know are probably wondering why they are suddenly so stressed. Actually, these palpitations are probably causing stress and not the other way around. These heartbeat flutters can be triggered by a drop in estrogen, which helps to regulate heartbeat, and by hot flashes, which keep you up at night and make you pant and hyperventilate during the day. Double-check with your physician, of course; and if it’s a perimenopause symptom, any technique that teaches you how to slow your heart rate, like diaphragmatic breathing, mindfulness, progressive relaxation, or yoga training, will help, giving you back your sense of control.5

article continues after advertisement

Brain Fog

“I’m losing it.” I hear it from my female friends, colleagues, and patients. I say it myself a lot. We are not talking about hot flashes, bladders that are always full, or thinning hair—we know that comes with perimenopause and beyond. We’re talking about forgetting our keys or phone, losing concentration and blanking on names, feeling dizzy and exhausted. Many experience brain fog before menopause even begins.6 Knowing you’re not alone can be reassuring, and knowing this may be part of perimenopause can lead you to initiate a conversation with your physician about addressing the brain fog.

Muscle Aches/Joint Pain

I didn’t know that the most frequently reported and prevalent perimenopause symptoms aren’t hot flashes or irregular periods—it is unexplained muscle and joint discomfort in shoulders, hips, knees, hands, and back.7 Because estrogen seems to be involved in controlling inflammation and repairing muscle cells, tendons, cartilage, and even bones, the hormone fluctuation during perimenopause can make us feel like we ran a marathon one day and are fine the next day. The answer, as you probably guessed, usually includes weight-bearing exercise to maintain muscle mass and rhythmic activities to help counteract and minimize these unexpected changes. If self-care is not enough to keep you active or to prevent pain, discuss physical therapy, medication, and/or hormone replacement therapy with your physician and decide together what works best for you.8

As I said before, my mother told me about menstruation, and my grandmother told me about menopause, but here’s what I tell my patients about perimenopause: The hormonal changes are not disasters. At any age and stage, they are inconveniences. When we think of it that way, we downgrade the label—and our reaction. This relabeling helped me. I hope it helps you.

item.title: Estrangement: Causes and Cures for Family Cutoffs
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Estrangement: Causes and Cures for Family Cutoffs

How common is estrangement, why does it happen, and how can families reconcile?

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • A poll indicates that 38 percent of US adults are currently estranged from at least one family member.
  • Reasons cited for estrangement include betrayal, lies, abuse, and conflicting beliefs and expectations.
  • Conflict can ensue when a member sees family hierarchy as crucial while another insists that behavior is key.
Source: Celine Cao / Unsplash

How common are cutoffs nowadays? In a 2025 YouGov poll of 4,395 U.S. adults, a whopping 38 percent were currently estranged from at least one family member. Sibling estrangement is the most common, with a prevalence of 24 percent, but 16 percent indicated a parent, 10 percent a child, 9 percent a grandparent, and 6 percent a grandchild (YouGov, 2025). Cornell's national survey found 27 percent of US adults had cut off contact with a relative, but estrangement from fathers is four times more common than from mothers—26 percent versus 6 percent in a nationally representative data set (Pillemer 2020). This striking statistic might reflect other dynamics not discussed here, such as parental alienation.

Why Estrangement Happens

The reasons most frequently cited for estrangement (YouGov, 2025) are manipulative behavior, betrayal, lies, physical/emotional abuse, and conflicting beliefs, values, and expectations. What sorts of beliefs, values, and expectations? Mismatches may center on differing notions of what duty, loyalty, growth, and emotional safety look like across generations within families. In a specific example, Reczek and colleagues (2023) found that smartphones can create “expectations of constant contact and connection within families” where family members find themselves “fielding regular requests for connection through texts, phone calls, and social media.” This can be experienced as stressful and poses an interesting challenge when it comes to establishing mutually agreed-upon boundaries.

Another Source of Conflict

Conflict can ensue “when one member insists that biological or origin ties and hierarchies reinforce the family unit, and another insists that behavior does” (Recsek and colleagues, 2023). Often the older generation points to age and hierarchy and insists, “We do things my way because that’s what’s always been done." Alternatively, younger generations seek to “redo” family ties and relations on the basis of being people first, and sons and daughters second.

Impacts of Estrangement

Research by Hank (2024) found that family estrangement is associated with lower life satisfaction, increased symptoms of depression, and grief over a loss of connection. Over time, members can experience regret for the years lost.

Reasons for Hope

Research indicates that 81 percent of adult children eventually reconcile with estranged mothers and 69 percent with estranged fathers (Reczek and colleagues, 2023). How can this happen? The trend across the vast majority of studies is that estrangement is typically temporary, not permanent. But a willingness to change and to find common ground is crucial to reconciliation. Patience and a repeatedly demonstrated capacity to listen and validate family members’ experiences, perceptions, wants, and needs are also critical.

Therapeutic Suggestions

Estranged members often feel confused, hurt, and angry, and may employ words from the helping professions as a sticky diagnostic label or accusation. “Toxic,” “narcissistic,” and “gaslighting” are prevalent terms that evoke a kind of moralization that makes compromise difficult.

“I” statements rather than “you” statements are another good idea in communication, as well as trying not to use absolutes such as “always” and “never.” When these terms are utilized, one recommendation is to pause before reacting with an immediate denial, dismissal, or minimization. People want to feel heard and emotionally validated.

Instead, family members can ask a question or seek further elaboration to find out what specific actions or behaviors felt toxic or abusive, and what a family member would want to see now for it to feel safer and to open space for a possible reconciliation. If an escalation can be avoided, both parties can attempt to focus on underlying conflicts around beliefs, values, and expectations and begin to create common ground in order to move forward.

item.title: How Does Pornography Affect Relationships?
item.description:
Pornography

How Does Pornography Affect Relationships?

Porn use impacts couples differently depending on why and how it is used.

Posted September 24, 2026

Key points
  • Shared viewing of pornography is generally positive for couples and can increase sexual communication.
  • Secret and frequent use of pornography often indicates unaddressed sexual differences within the couple.
  • Helping couples talk about pornography and their sexual values can increase congruence and decrease conflict.
Source: Image by Jupi Lu from Pixabay

Conversations about pornography often begin with a simple question: Is it good or bad for a relationship?

Research suggests that this may be the wrong question. Pornography use is not consistently linked to either positive or negative outcomes for couples. Instead, its effects depend on why it is used, whether partners know about it, and whether it fits within the couple’s agreements and values.

When pornography use may have positive effects

For some couples, pornography is associated with greater sexual communication, exploration, and satisfaction. More favorable outcomes happen when partners use it together, both genuinely want to participate, and feel comfortable talking about porn and sexuality in general.

Pornography may give couples a way to discuss their sexual fantasies, preferences, or activities. It can also provide novelty or sexual stimulation and help some people better understand their interests.

Couples in which both partners privately use pornography at comparable levels often report greater closeness and communication than couples with very different patterns of use. This doesn’t mean that couples must use pornography equally, but the goal is for them to have greater congruence in their sexual attitudes and expectations.

Some studies suggest that women’s pornography use coincides with greater sexual desire and an increased likelihood of partnered sexual activity. However, people use pornography for different reasons, and gender differences may reflect social expectations, preferred content, relationship dynamics, or motivation.

When pornography use may create problems

Less favorable outcomes occur when partners disagree about whether pornography is acceptable, when use is hidden, or when one person uses it much more frequently than the other.

A partner may experience concealed use as betrayal, particularly if the couple has never clearly discussed whether pornography falls inside or outside their definition of fidelity. Even when the user views the behavior as private and harmless, their partner may experience it as exclusion, comparison, rejection, or a violation of trust. Higher levels of solitary porn use may indicate unaddressed desire discrepancy and exacerbate sexual dissatisfaction in the marriage.

article continues after advertisement

When porn use is secret, some porn users themselves report lower satisfaction and intimacy. When their partners know about the use, it sometimes increases sexual intimacy, possibly because disclosure created an opportunity for openness about desires. Partners, however, do not always see this as a positive. Disclosure of porn use may reduce secrecy without automatically resolving feelings of hurt or exclusion.

Differences in desire can become entangled with pornography use. If one partner wants sex more frequently, pornography may serve as an additional sexual outlet and may decrease sexual pressure on a partner—however, the other partner sometimes sees it as evidence that they are unwanted or inadequate. The central issue is the difference in desire—not pornography.

Source: Image by Silviu on the street from Pixabay

Motivation and meaning make a difference

Pornography used for curiosity, pleasure, or self-exploration is generally associated with more favorable outcomes than pornography used to escape negative emotions or relationship difficulties.

Using pornography occasionally to relax is not necessarily a problem. But concern can be appropriate when it is a person’s primary way of coping with loneliness, anxiety, depression, shame, or dissatisfaction. Emotional avoidance may temporarily reduce discomfort while leaving the underlying problem untouched and allowing conflict to fester.

When pornography use conflicts strongly with someone’s religious, moral, or sexual beliefs, or with their partner’s morals, the resulting shame may contribute to lower sexual and relationship satisfaction.

The distress is real, but it does not necessarily mean that pornography is the problem. Treatment should respect values while helping people to distinguish between accountability and global self-condemnation.

Attachment patterns may matter as well. One study found that greater pornography use was associated with lower relationship satisfaction among anxiously attached women but slightly higher satisfaction among anxiously attached men. Findings like these highlight why clinicians should avoid assuming that the same behavior has the same psychological meaning for every person.

article continues after advertisement

What couples can do

Couples may benefit from discussing pornography before conflict develops. Useful questions include:

  • What does pornography mean to each of us?
  • Do we consider it private sexual behavior, shared sexual behavior, or a form of infidelity?
  • What kinds of use feel acceptable or unacceptable?
  • Are our agreements freely chosen, realistic, and mutual?
  • Is pornography supporting our sexual relationship, replacing it, or helping us avoid difficult conversations?
  • Is either partner feeling pressured, controlled, ashamed, deceived, or rejected?

There is no single agreement that works for every couple. The goal is not to impose a universal rule but to create clear expectations that respect both partners’ autonomy and boundaries.

Source: Image by Sasin Tipchai from Pixabay

Implications for therapy

Treatment should focus on the problem the couple is actually experiencing and view the conflict over porn as a potential indicator of unresolved conflict and disagreements related to sex and intimacy.

  • Boundary conflicts may require clearer agreements about privacy and fidelity.
  • Desire differences may call for conversations about sexual needs and expectations.
  • Shame related to moral beliefs may benefit from values-sensitive work.
  • Emotionally avoidant use may require healthier coping strategies.

Couples therapy may be especially helpful because relationship distress can sometimes contribute to pornography use, just as pornography-related conflict can contribute to distress. Research has found that general relationship education may produce small reductions in pornography use even when pornography is not directly targeted, probably through reducing relationship conflict.

article continues after advertisement

The clearest conclusion is that pornography’s impact on a couple depends on consent, openness, motivation, personal values, partner compatibility, and the broader health of the relationship.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.
